title: Discussion Tracker: Supporting Teacher Learning about Students’ Collaborative Argumentation in High School Classrooms
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of helping K-12 teachers learn to facilitate collaborative argumentation in classroom discussions, a skill that many teachers find difficult to develop. The authors present Discussion Tracker (DT), a classroom discussion analytics system that uses NLP to automatically code student talk along three dimensions: argument moves, specificity, and collaboration. DT then generates visualizations and feedback such as annotated transcripts, collaboration maps, strengths/weaknesses summaries, and planning support for the next discussion.

The system was evaluated in high school English Language Arts classrooms. Eighteen teachers from four schools each led a discussion on a literary text; their discussions were recorded, transcribed, manually annotated, and then used to evaluate DT. Teachers used DT after a brief demo and completed surveys plus 45-minute cognitive interviews while reviewing their students’ discussions. The NLP classifiers were also tested against human annotations from the collected corpus.

The study found that teachers perceived DT as useful for reflecting on student discussion and for identifying strengths and weaknesses in facilitation, with generally high usability ratings. The automated classifiers achieved moderate to substantial agreement with human labels for argument moves and specificity, but collaboration prediction was weaker for some classes, especially agree and challenge/probe. The paper concludes that discussion analytics can support teacher learning, while noting the need for further model improvement, more data collection, automated transcription/segmentation, and interface refinement.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a small classroom deployment with usability evaluation and model benchmark results, not a randomized or quasi-experimental impact study. The evidence is qualitative/survey-based with classifier validation, so it meets only limited credibility criteria for outcome impact claims.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports high teacher-perceived usefulness but does not measure student learning gains or provide causal impact estimates. Any impact is therefore modest and unclear, with no effect size meeting a medium/large threshold.

interventions.use_case: classroom discussion analytics system (Discussion Tracker) using NLP classifiers to code teacher-recorded high school discussion transcripts for argument moves, specificity, and collaboration, then generate visual analytics and planning support for teacher reflection

finding.finding_summary: Teachers reported that Discussion Tracker was very helpful for learning to facilitate collaborative argumentation in high school literature discussions. On the usability survey (n=18 teachers), nine of 13 items had a mean of 4.5/5 or higher, including strong ratings for the annotated transcript (mean=4.89), pie charts (mean=4.78), and overall helpfulness for teaching literature discussions (mean=4.72).
finding.measure: Teacher usability/perceived usefulness survey ratings; Likert-scale items on support for collaborative argumentation facilitation

finding.finding_summary: The system was perceived as helping teachers recognize student strengths and weaknesses and giving them more insight than they usually get from reflecting on discussion, suggesting workflow support for analysis and planning. Teachers also rated the goal-setting and instructional resources favorably, though ease of use was slightly lower than other features (mean=4.11).
finding.measure: Teacher survey ratings of system usefulness for recognizing strengths/weaknesses, gaining insight, and supporting goal-setting/planning
